shots.narration_paragraph: Titanic's designers had given the vessel watertight compartments as a defense against accidents. To understand why that defense failed, forget for a moment the sweeping camera shot of a ship slipping under the sea. Imagine standing inside one flooded forward compartment. Water presses through a damaged part of the hull. The level begins to rise. A bulkhead ahead of you seems to stop the flow. But that wall has a top. If the ship's bow settles far enough, water can eventually pass over the boundary into the compartment behind it. A barrier that works at one angle becomes ineffective as the ship changes trim.

shots.narration_paragraph: The British inquiry's technical findings were precise about one threshold. Titanic could survive certain limited combinations of flooding, including the flooding of two adjacent compartments under its specified design assumptions. It could not stay afloat with the four forward compartments and boiler room number six flooded as they were after the accident. The fact that the bow was drawing more and more water meant that the ship's own sinking posture increased the extent of the danger. It was a progressive problem, not one small puncture that could simply be plugged with a blanket.

shots.narration_paragraph: The immediate physical consequences were hard to see from the passenger decks. Water entering a ship adds weight, but it is not weight in the ordinary sense of cargo loaded safely above the keel. It removes the buoyant volume that keeps the hull floating, and the distribution of that loss matters. As the forward compartments flooded, Titanic's bow sank lower. This brought parts of the vessel that had previously been clear of the sea closer to the surface. Flooding could then extend where the designers had not intended it.

shots.narration_paragraph: There are accounts of engineers and crew working as the emergency developed. Pumps could move water from some spaces, and the ship had machinery intended to handle flooding under limited conditions. But pumps have capacities, and a damaged vessel can admit seawater faster than it can be removed. The central question was not whether any pump existed. It was whether all the available defenses together could cope with the actual rate and distribution of the flooding. The answer became increasingly clear as the minutes passed.

shots.narration_paragraph: The British report tried to assess exactly what had been damaged, using observations and testimony gathered after the ship itself had vanished. This creates a problem for any modern filmmaker. We may draw a cutaway diagram showing approximate compartments and the bow settling, but it cannot be introduced as an eyewitness photograph. Much of the underwater damage was not measured while the ship was still afloat. A convincing visualization must make its assumptions visible instead of hiding them behind beautiful textures.

shots.narration_paragraph: Some stories emphasize the rivets, the steel, or the exceptionally cold sea as if one material defect explains everything. Material science can help investigators understand damage mechanisms, and researchers have debated various structural vulnerabilities. But the period inquiry's core conclusion did not depend on discovering a single defective rivet. Titanic had made contact with ice, water entered multiple compartments, and the ship's subdivision could not contain the resulting flood. To elevate a theory about one component into the entire explanation would obscure those established facts.

shots.narration_paragraph: The weight of the bow also changed life above decks. Stairways no longer sat at exactly the same angle. Floors slowly acquired a slope. Water reached places where it had never belonged. People who had doubted the emergency might notice that the ship was becoming harder to ignore. Yet these changes were gradual enough at first to encourage another dangerous thought: perhaps Titanic would settle but remain afloat. An ocean liner that still carried electric light, still had familiar corridors, and still towered above the sea could be difficult to abandon.

shots.narration_paragraph: Thomas Andrews, one of the ship's principal designers, has often been portrayed making an immediate calculation and realizing she was doomed. Accounts associate him with assessing the damage, but the exact words and sequence portrayed in films should not be accepted uncritically. It is a reasonable engineering inference that serious progressive flooding would soon demonstrate a fatal condition. A documentary should not transform that inference into an invented verbatim speech.

shots.narration_paragraph: As midnight approached, the need for an evacuation was becoming urgent. The rescue equipment had to be readied, and the vessel's wireless operators had a vital task. They could alert the world to a ship sinking in the North Atlantic. But an emergency signal cannot make a distant vessel appear alongside. There were still miles of dark sea between Titanic and any possible help.
